chapter_theme: The breaking of self-containment (நிறை). Desire is an axe against a door, a sneeze that can't be held back, a tyrant working her at midnight. The chapter ends with a woman who sets out to sulk and finds her heart has already gone over to him.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar has her reply to her friend's appeals for restraint (1251-1256), and then account for how she has yielded after he returned, in his setting from the courtesans (1257-1260).

1251.reading: The woman says that the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint, bolted with the bar of shame.
1251.nuance: The architecture is exact, as Parimelazhagar explains: restraint is the door that keeps what is inside from being taken, shame is the bolt, since restraint holds as long as shame does. Manakkudavar has அறிவு, 'understanding', as the door, though the verse says நிறை.

1252.reading: The woman says that this thing called desire has no pity, for it puts her heart to work even at midnight.
1252.nuance: The image is forced labour: everyone else's work stops at midnight, and hers doesn't. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar identify the task as sending the heart to him, which, Parimelazhagar notes, isn't a proper task for a woman, and is why she says 'this thing called desire'.

1253.reading: The woman says she would hide her desire, but like a sneeze it comes out without her intending it.
1253.nuance: The comparison is deliberately undignified. குறிப்பின்றி means without intent, using a word that in chapter 110 named her coded signs, which were deliberate. Now the sign sends itself.

1254.reading: The woman says she used to say she had restraint, yet her desire passes beyond concealment and comes out in public.
1254.nuance: The tense matters, on Parimelazhagar's gloss: 'until today I thought of myself as restrained'. She has lost not only the restraint but also a belief about who she is.

1255.reading: The woman says the greatness of not going after one who has turned hostile is something those who are sick with love can't know.
1255.nuance: Honour isn't rejected, but it's placed out of reach. Parimelazhagar gives the other half: those who don't have the sickness can know it, and he calls them the people of honour (மானம் உடையார்). He also softens going after to continual thought, and softens செற்றார், 'enemy', as one who has made time painful.

1256.reading: The woman exclaims, in irony, how fine is the grief that has come to her, making her want to go after one who has turned hostile.
1256.nuance: Both older commentators hear sarcasm in அளித்து, 'sweet', as they did in the night verse 1168, meaning the opposite. Her comment on her own condition has become a dry detachment.

1257.reading: The woman says she knows nothing of shame when the man she loves does in desire what she longs for.

positions.position: The context is that he has returned from courtesans; the shame she failed to feel is shame at touching a chest they have touched.
positions.quote: நாண் - பரத்தையர் தோய்ந்த மார்பைத் தோய்தற்கு நாணுதல்.

positions.position: It's a general statement on women and desire, and doesn't mention any courtesans.

1258.reading: The woman says that the soft speech of that thief of many deceptions is the weapon that breaks her womanhood.
1258.nuance: The chapter's picture of siege ends here, with Parimelazhagar glossing பெண்மை as restraint, a fortress taken by words. She knows them to be deceptive, and that doesn't protect her. பணிமொழி was how he praised her, in 1121.

1259.reading: The woman says she went away meaning to sulk, and embraced him when she saw her heart beginning to join with him.
1259.nuance: She didn't yield to him but to her heart, and embracing is what's left when her instrument defects. Parimelazhagar says it exactly: the heart that is the means of sulking has itself turned into the means of joining.

1260.reading: The woman asks whether those whose hearts are like fat thrown in a fire can ever say 'we will join and then hold out in a sulk'.
1260.nuance: An extraordinary image of unlovely and total melting: not wax or butter, but animal fat.

positions.position: புணர்ந்து here means simply coming close, or meeting; sulking fails at first encounter.
The word means after union; one can't then keep up the quarrel.
positions.quote: கூடிக் களித்தபின் ஊடல் கொண்டு அதில் உறுதியாக இருக்க முடியுமா?.

links.note: 966 asks what could be gained, neither fame nor heaven, by going after those who despise you. 1255 is a direct reply from inside love: people with this sickness can't know that kind of honour. The ethics chapter on honour isn't refuted, but declared unavailable.

The sneeze appears in two contrary ways: in 1203 it threatens and doesn't come, which she reads as him not thinking of her. In 1253 it comes uncontrollably, like her desire. So his love fails to arrive and hers can't be stopped.

The same phrase, மறையிறந்து மன்று படும், in both. 1138 presents it as a general truth about women's love, with Parimelazhagar seeing her own case in it. In 1254 she says it in the first person, having once thought herself an exception.
Both tell the same story in the first person: she went to sulk, and her heart went to join him. Whichever is read first, the second confirms that this is a repeating pattern, and that she knows it.

source_issues: 1260: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts at புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல், so his headnote and gloss are missing.
1252: Parimelazhagar's note has a stray question mark and a garbled phrase, தொழிலின்கண்ணேயாடல் ?- ... தாயைப் பணி கோடல், where தன்னைப் பணி கோடல் seems intended.
1253, 1254: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption in வௌ¢ப்பட்டே and வௌ¢ப்படா.
